I think it'd be an interesting experiment for someone to try to launch a Prove2Me campaign to autoformalize this 2012 paper that also uses the Circle Method: https://arxiv.org/abs/1201.6656.

I'd be most interested in someone who's never used Prove2Me before doing it. #FLT > Anthropic Vinogradov experiment has everything I figured out about how to do this sort of thing in the experiment I ran this week on older results I'd rememebered from my period as a budding mathematician.
I'm keen to give it a shot. I've never used Prove2Me before, can try running this on my own little Claude / Codex loops overnight.

Tim Abbott said:

I'd be most interested in someone who's never used Prove2Me before doing it.

I'd be interested in seeing lots of people doing it simultaneously. To me, part of the advantage of a system like Prove2Me is that is should facilitate lots of people to contribute to auto-formalization projects with little-to-no central organization.
How is this aspect different from Tau Ceti?

I don't know much about Tau Ceti. I think in an ideal world, some experiments would answer the question of what aspects of these platforms make them better for autoformalization work, and use that to make one really good platform. I think for this thread, I'm just interested in generating more data on what is possible with Prove2Me using consumer accounts, which might help answer questions about whether it has any key features/ideas that Tau Ceti should adopt, or similar questions like that.

I don't believe we need several autoformalization databases, we just need one really good one.
This is a social problem as well as an engineering one though.

How is this aspect different from Tau Ceti?

Here's some differences I've noticed:

  1. prove2me strongly encourages a "top-down" workflow where a theorem is broken down into subgoals, and a unit of incremental work is "breaking down a theorem into sub-goals". Tau Ceti is a "bottom-up" workflow - an incremental unit of work is a PR, which builds theorems on top of previously proven theorems.
  2. submitting incremental work to prove2me (breaking down a theorem into subgoals) does not require human approval. in contrast, Tau Ceti requires that PRs follow a roadmap, and editing roadmaps require human review and approval.

(this is not a comment about which approach is "better", or even if they have the same goals! just listing out what I see as the biggest differences)

For those who'd like to contribute:

https://prove2.me/missions/Every%20Odd%20Number%20Greater%20Than%201%20is%20the%20Sum%20of%20at%20Most%20Five%20Primes

Does prove2me have any quality control on the code? I've been trying it out and It doesnt seem so, that seems to be a big difference with Tau Ceti, which for example wouldn't allow any max heartbeat overrides. I think for fast formalisation of some paper or headline result then prove2me seems like a good option, but its less clear to me that you can do much with the resulting code directly. It also doesnt seem to have an option to build on top of Tau Ceti, which would seem like an easy win since that will make future projects easier to formalise (compared to starting from mathlib).
Also, do you plan on regularly bumping the repo to use newer versions of mathlib?

One thing that I've mentioned before is that we've seen lots of benefits from taking an existing autoformalisation and PRing it to Tau Ceti. The code that comes out is usually much nicer and a lot more reusable (it sees starting fresh and building from the ground up is quite a good way to clean code). I think one option for collaboration would be to have some pipeline where a completed prove2me project then takes the bits of general interest and becomes a roadmap on Tau Ceti (or contributes to an existing roadmap). One could then "port over" the proof which would likely improve the code.
I pointed my personal agent at this project, and it told me some agent had uploaded a proof strategy that was a reduction ... to the Goldbach conjecture.

Currently we don’t have much quality control for intermediate theorems or proof sketches. We are playing with ideas of “reporting” theorems that don’t say what they mean, or adding some sort of reputation system. I’d love to hear ideas in this direction.
I don’t know how to integrate best with Tau Ceti, but I’d love to find a way to do this!

Right now, each theorem (and mission) is on a fixed version of Lean and Mathlib. We do want to periodically update Lean and Mathlib to get upstream changes. How should we best support multiple versions of Lean and Mathlib? Do you want to choose a version when you propose a mission? Should we try to upgrade existing theorems to newer versions of Lean/Mathlib (are there good tools for this?)
I feel like ideally the platform would just periodically bulk-update everything to a new version, but that would require having some team of agents to do the upgrades.

I ran GPT-6 Astra in a loop pointed towards this mission.

It wrote 2 accepted theorems!

But it got stuck on a third. On submission it got an error response: "Verification timed out after 300s.” Seems like it is an eng issue on Prove2Me's end?
We have a setting so proof sketch can only compile for 5min on prove2me’s servers. Can you ask your agent to break the statement into smaller pieces?

Okay sounds good, will give it a try

For the API, just an idea, the error response could mention the recommendation of breaking down the statement into smaller pieces so that an agent is automatically steered towards it
Asked the agent to break the statement into smaller pieces and it proved 2 more theorems
